## DP: the six lines (4)

<p class="rev-plan">Before any DP code, these are written as comments in the editor. Say all six for the card, then open and check the order.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-six">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DP</span><span class="rev-q">The six lines to write as comments before any DP code?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

```text
STATE       dp[...] = <a NUMBER or BOOLEAN in words>, e.g. "fewest coins to make amount a"
QUESTION    best (min/max) | possible (or) | count (+)
CHOICES     what can I do at this state? (take/skip · which coin · 1 or 2 steps · from above/left)
TRANSITION  each choice leads to which smaller state? combine with min/max, or, +
BASE        the smallest state whose answer I already know (dp[0] = ?)
ORDER       which states must exist before dp[i]? -> fill direction (forward, backward, by length)
```

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-six">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-question">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DP</span><span class="rev-q">QUESTION: which words mean best, possible or count, and what operator and starting value follow?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

| Words in the problem | Kind | Combine with | Unknown starts as |
|---|---|---|---|
| minimum, fewest, cheapest, shortest | best | `min` | `inf` (or amount+1) |
| maximum, most, largest, longest, max profit | best | `max` | `0` or `-inf` |
| can, possible, exists, reachable | possible | `or` | `False` |
| how many ways, count, number of paths | count | `+` | `0` |

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-question">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-order">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DP</span><span class="rev-q">ORDER: which direction do you fill, and the three loop rules for coins and knapsack?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

If `dp[i]` uses smaller indices, fill forward; if it uses larger (suffix DPs), fill backward; 2-D fills row by row. Two rules that matter for coins/knapsack:

- **Reuse allowed** (unlimited coins): iterate amounts **forward** within a coin.
- **Each item once** (0/1 knapsack): iterate amounts **backward** so the item is not reused.
- **Counting**: order matters (permutations) → amount loop outside, coins inside; order does not matter (combinations) → coins outside, amounts inside.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-order">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-families">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DP</span><span class="rev-q">The DP families and their shapes?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

| Family | Shape |
|---|---|
| Fibonacci-style | `dp[i]` from a few previous |
| Take / skip | best(skip, take) |
| Unbounded choice | `dp[a] <- dp[a - choice]` |
| Ending-at | `dp[i]` = best ending at i, answer = max over i |
| Grid | from above + from left |
| Two sequences | match → diagonal, else drop one side |
| Expand / interval | center or `dp[l][r]` |

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-families">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Patterns: cues to name (21)

<p class="rev-plan">The question side shows only the cues, the phrases a problem statement uses. Say the pattern name, its core idea and the complexity out loud, then open. If you cannot name it in ten seconds, it is not known.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-advanced-graph">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'weighted', 'minimum cost', 'cheapest path', 'network delay', 'connect all points', 'k stops' · Edge weights present; BFS no longer correct</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Advanced Graph / Shortest Path.** Weighted shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, ordering under constraints beyond simple BFS. Blind 75 touches this only through Alien Dictionary; know the shapes for follow-ups.

**Ask yourself.**

- Are weights non-negative (Dijkstra) or possibly negative (Bellman-Ford)?
- Single source or all pairs?
- Is it really MST (connect everything cheaply) rather than shortest path?
- Constraint on number of edges (k stops → BFS layers / Bellman-Ford k rounds)?

**Core idea.** Dijkstra: once a node is popped with the smallest tentative distance, that distance is final (non-negative weights). MST: the cheapest edge crossing a cut is safe.

**Shape.** Dijkstra: heap of (dist, node); pop; skip stale; relax neighbours. Prim: heap of edges from the tree. Kruskal: sort edges + union-find.

**Complexity.** Dijkstra O((V+E) log V); Bellman-Ford O(V·E); Kruskal O(E log E).

**Traps.**

- Using BFS with weights
- Not skipping stale heap entries
- Dijkstra with negative edges
- Confusing shortest-path tree with MST

**Not this when.** Unweighted → BFS. DAG ordering → topological sort. Connectivity only → union-find.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-advanced-graph">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-arrays-hashing">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'duplicate', 'anagram', 'group', 'frequency', 'top k', 'pair that sums to' · Unsorted input and a hint that O(n log n) is not good enough · Need to look something up 'have I seen X before?' while scanning once</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Arrays / Hashing.** Any question about membership, counting, grouping, or finding pairs/complements in unsorted data where O(n) is expected.

**Ask yourself.**

- What is the key I need O(1) lookup on: value, complement, canonical form, count?
- Am I counting, grouping, or checking existence?
- Is the value range small enough for an array instead of a hash map (bucket idea)?

**Core idea.** Trade space for time: a hash map turns a nested search into a constant-time lookup, so one pass suffices.

**Shape.** Scan once; for each element compute a key; consult/update the map; answer derived from the map at the end or on the fly.

**Complexity.** Time O(n) (O(n·k) when the key costs k to build); space O(n) or O(alphabet).

**Traps.**

- Inserting before checking (element pairs with itself)
- Unhashable keys (lists) — use tuples/strings
- Forgetting a bounded value range enables counting sort / buckets
- Sorting when the problem forbids or when O(n) is expected

**Not this when.** Input is sorted or must be processed in place with O(1) space → two pointers or in-place marking. Order/adjacency matters → sliding window or stack.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-arrays-hashing">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-backtracking">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'all combinations', 'all subsets', 'exists a path', 'word in grid', 'unlimited reuse', 'no reuse' · Exponential output or search space with pruning opportunities · Choices at each step, then undo</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Backtracking.** Enumerate all combinations/permutations/paths under constraints; search a grid for a word; build candidates incrementally and undo.

**Ask yourself.**

- What is the state at each recursion (index, remaining target, path so far, visited)?
- How do I avoid generating the same combination in a different order (start index)?
- What prunes early (remaining < 0, prefix not in trie)?

**Core idea.** Choose → explore → un-choose; ordering constraints (start index) prevent duplicates; pruning cuts dead branches.

**Shape.** def bt(state): if goal: record; return; for choice in choices(state): apply; bt(new_state); undo.

**Complexity.** Time exponential (O(k^depth) or O(4·3^(L-1)) on grids); space O(depth).

**Traps.**

- Forgetting to undo (unmark visited, pop path)
- Generating permutations when combinations were asked
- No pruning → TLE
- Copying the path instead of referencing then copying on record

**Not this when.** Counting the number of ways (not listing them) → DP. Shortest path → BFS. Optimal value with overlapping subproblems → DP.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-backtracking">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-binary-search">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'sorted', 'rotated', 'O(log n)', 'find minimum/target', 'first/last position' · A yes/no predicate that is false…false,true…true over the search space (binary search on the answer) · Search space is a numeric range, not just an array</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Binary Search.** Sorted or rotated-sorted data, or any monotonic predicate over a range where the answer can be found by halving.

**Ask yourself.**

- What is monotonic here — the values, or a predicate on the index/answer?
- After comparing mid, which half can I prove does NOT contain the answer?
- Am I searching for existence, a boundary (first true), or an extremum?

**Core idea.** Each comparison halves the space while preserving the invariant that the answer stays inside [lo, hi].

**Shape.** lo, hi = bounds; while lo < hi (or <=): mid; test; move lo or hi so the invariant holds; return lo/hi with a final check.

**Complexity.** Time O(log n); space O(1).

**Traps.**

- Infinite loop from mid rounding with lo = mid
- Wrong invariant for inclusive vs exclusive hi
- Rotated arrays: identify the sorted half before deciding
- Duplicates break the 'which half is sorted' test

**Not this when.** Data unsorted with no monotonic predicate → hashing/sorting first. Need all matches, not one → scan or two pointers.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-binary-search">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-bst-inorder">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'BST', 'binary search tree', 'kth smallest/largest', 'sorted order', 'lowest common ancestor' with BST · Left < node < right must hold for entire subtrees</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**BST / Inorder.** Binary search tree questions: kth smallest, validation, LCA, range queries — the ordering property is the tool.

**Ask yourself.**

- Does inorder traversal (sorted sequence) solve it directly?
- Can I use the BST property to descend in O(h) instead of visiting everything?
- What bounds must each node satisfy relative to all ancestors?

**Core idea.** Inorder of a BST is sorted; comparisons at a node tell you which subtree contains what you want.

**Shape.** Iterative inorder with a stack (stop early at k); or descend from root comparing values; or DFS carrying (low, high) bounds.

**Complexity.** Time O(h) for descents, O(h + k) for kth via inorder, O(n) for full validation; space O(h).

**Traps.**

- Validating only against direct children
- Equal values (strict vs non-strict)
- Using ±infinity sentinels incorrectly
- Collecting the whole inorder list when early stop was possible

**Not this when.** Tree is not a BST → general DFS/BFS. Need frequent kth queries with updates → augmented tree/order statistics (out of scope).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-bst-inorder">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-dp-1d">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'number of ways', 'minimum/maximum … ending at', 'can be segmented', 'fewest coins', 'non-adjacent', 'decode', 'longest increasing subsequence' · Recursion with repeated states; greedy is wrong · Answer builds from smaller prefixes or smaller amounts</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**1-D Dynamic Programming.** Optimal value or count over a sequence/amount where the answer for position i depends on a few earlier positions; overlapping subproblems. Before any DP attempt: the six questions in the DP cheat sheet.

**Ask yourself.**

- What is dp[i] in one sentence (ways to reach i? best ending at i? feasible prefix i?)
- What are the last-step choices that lead to i, and from which states?
- Base cases and answer location (dp[n] or max over dp)?
- Can I roll the array to O(1) space?

**Core idea.** Define the state so the last decision is local; the recurrence combines a constant (or small) number of earlier states; memoise or fill bottom-up.

**Shape.** dp array sized n+1 (or amount+1) → base cases → for i in range: dp[i] = combine(dp[i−k] for valid k) → return dp[n] / max.

**Complexity.** Time O(n·choices) (O(n²) for LIS-style, O(amount·coins) for knapsack-like); space O(n) or O(1) rolled.

**Traps.**

- Wrong state definition (ending-at vs up-to)
- Greedy shortcut that fails (coin change)
- Off-by-one on indices with a padded dp[0]
- Forgetting the min/max tracking pair when negatives flip signs (product problems)

**Not this when.** Two sequences or a grid → 2-D DP. Need to enumerate solutions → backtracking. Local choice provably safe → greedy.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-dp-1d">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-dp-2d">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'two strings', 'common subsequence', 'grid paths', 'm × n', 'edit', 'match' · Recurrence depends on (i−1, j), (i, j−1), (i−1, j−1)</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**2-D Dynamic Programming.** Two sequences (LCS, edit distance) or a grid (paths) where the state needs two indices.

**Ask yourself.**

- What does dp[i][j] mean (prefixes of length i and j? cell (i, j)?)
- What happens when the current characters match vs not?
- Can I keep one row (previous) to reduce space?
- Is there a closed form (combinatorics) for the grid case?

**Core idea.** Matching last elements extends the diagonal state; otherwise take the best of dropping one side; grids sum the two arrivals.

**Shape.** dp with (m+1)×(n+1) padding → fill row by row → dp[m][n]; roll rows for O(n) space.

**Complexity.** Time O(m·n); space O(m·n) or O(min(m, n)).

**Traps.**

- Subsequence vs substring confusion
- Padding off-by-one
- Wrong combination for mismatch (max vs sum)
- Trying 1-D when two indices are genuinely needed

**Not this when.** Single sequence → 1-D DP. Palindromes in one string → expand-around-center is usually simpler than 2-D DP.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-dp-2d">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-graph-dfs-bfs">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'connected', 'islands', 'reachable', 'clone', 'grid of 0/1', 'neighbors', 'shortest number of steps' · Nodes and edges are explicit, or implicit in a grid</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Graph DFS / BFS.** Connectivity, components, reachability, flood fill on grids, cloning, shortest path in unweighted graphs.

**Ask yourself.**

- What is a node and what is an edge (grid cells with 4-neighbours)?
- DFS (any path, components) or BFS (shortest path, levels)?
- How do I mark visited — a set, or in place on the grid?
- Can I start from the borders/targets instead of every cell (multi-source, reverse search)?

**Core idea.** Each node is discovered once; a visited set (or in-place marking) guarantees O(V+E).

**Shape.** for each unvisited start: traverse (stack/recursion or queue), mark visited, collect; count/aggregate per traversal.

**Complexity.** Time O(V+E) = O(m·n) on grids; space O(V) for visited/queue.

**Traps.**

- Recursion depth on large grids (use iterative or BFS)
- Diagonal vs 4-directional adjacency
- Forgetting the visited map for cycles when cloning
- Simulating from every source instead of reversing from the targets

**Not this when.** Ordering constraints → topological sort. Weighted shortest path → Dijkstra. Only components count without traversal → union-find.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-graph-dfs-bfs">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-greedy">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'maximum/minimum with a simple structure', 'can reach', 'minimum removals', 'max profit one transaction', 'maximum subarray' · An exchange argument works: swapping the greedy choice for any other never helps</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Greedy.** Local choice that is provably safe: earliest finishing interval, farthest reach, running max/min, Kadane-style 'reset when negative'.

**Ask yourself.**

- What quantity, if I always pick the extreme, can never be worse (exchange argument)?
- Is there a running summary (max reach, min price, current sum) that decides each step?
- Would DP be equivalent but slower — can I explain why greedy is safe?

**Core idea.** A locally optimal step preserves the possibility of a globally optimal completion; one linear scan with a running summary suffices.

**Shape.** Sort if needed → scan → maintain summary (best so far, current run, farthest reach) → update answer each step.

**Complexity.** Time O(n) or O(n log n) with sort; space O(1).

**Traps.**

- Assuming greedy works without the exchange argument (coin change is the classic failure)
- Initialising with 0 when all values may be negative
- Sorting by the wrong key
- Confusing with the harder variant (Jump Game II, multiple transactions)

**Not this when.** Choices interact and local optimum can be wrong → DP. Need all solutions → backtracking.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-greedy">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-heap">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'k smallest/largest', 'k sorted lists', 'median of stream', 'minimum rooms', 'schedule', 'most frequent' · Need extract-min/max in O(log n) while inserting · Only the extremes matter, not full sorted order</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Heap / Priority Queue.** Repeatedly need the current min/max among a changing set: k-way merge, top-k, medians, scheduling by earliest end.

**Ask yourself.**

- Do I need the full sort, or just the extreme repeatedly?
- Min-heap or max-heap, and of what tuple (with tie-breakers)?
- Would two heaps (low/high halves) or a heap of size k solve it?

**Core idea.** A heap keeps the extreme available in O(1) and restores order in O(log n) per change; a size-k heap keeps the k best seen so far.

**Shape.** Build heap of initial items → loop: pop extreme, process, push replacement/new items → answer from heap contents or pop sequence.

**Complexity.** Time O(n log k) or O(n log n); space O(k) or O(n).

**Traps.**

- Python heapq is a min-heap: negate for max
- Tuple comparison hitting incomparable objects (add an index tie-breaker)
- Rebalancing direction in two-heap median
- Using a heap when bucket counting gives O(n)

**Not this when.** Value range small → bucket sort. Need arbitrary deletes or order statistics → balanced BST/sorted container. Only one pass extreme → single variable.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-heap">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-intervals">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'intervals', 'meetings', 'overlapping', 'merge', 'rooms', 'non-overlapping' · Sorting by start or by end makes the problem a single sweep</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Intervals.** Ranges with start/end: merge, insert, count overlaps, minimum removals, minimum rooms, can-attend.

**Ask yourself.**

- Sort by start (merging, overlap checks) or by end (greedy selection)?
- What is the overlap condition exactly (inclusive ends?)
- Do I need the maximum concurrent count (sweep line / two sorted arrays / heap)?

**Core idea.** After sorting, each interval interacts only with the current merged/last-kept interval (or the earliest-ending active one).

**Shape.** Sort → iterate → compare with last kept: merge/extend, skip, or count → return result.

**Complexity.** Time O(n log n); space O(n) output or O(1).

**Traps.**

- Not taking max of ends when merging
- Touching intervals treated as overlapping or not — clarify
- Greedy by wrong key (keep longest instead of earliest end)
- Tie order in sweep line (end before start at equal time when touching is allowed)

**Not this when.** Intervals on a tree/graph → different structure. Need dynamic insert/query of overlaps → interval tree / segment tree (rare in interviews).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-intervals">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-linked-list">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'linked list', 'in place', 'O(1) space', 'reverse', 'merge', 'cycle', 'nth from end' · The task decomposes into: find middle, reverse, merge, two-pointer gap · Node identity matters more than values</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Linked List Pointer Manipulation.** Singly linked list rewiring: reverse, merge, find middle, detect cycle, remove nth-from-end, reorder — usually in O(1) extra space.

**Ask yourself.**

- Which of the four primitives (reverse, merge, middle via fast/slow, gap pointers) does this compose?
- Do I need a dummy head to avoid head/edge special cases?
- Which pointer must be saved before I overwrite a .next?

**Core idea.** Never lose a reference: save next before rewiring; a dummy head makes head-removal ordinary.

**Shape.** dummy → pointers (prev/cur/next or slow/fast) → loop with explicit save-then-rewire → return dummy.next.

**Complexity.** Time O(n); space O(1) iterative (O(n) recursive stack).

**Traps.**

- Losing the rest of the list by rewiring before saving next
- Not cutting the first half's tail before reversing the second half (creates a cycle)
- Null checks on fast.next
- Off-by-one in the gap for nth-from-end

**Not this when.** Random access or sorting needed → arrays. Values (not structure) matter → hashing is acceptable when space is allowed.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-linked-list">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-matrix-traversal">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'rotate the image', 'spiral order', 'set row and column to zero', 'in place', 'O(1) extra space' · The answer is about index gymnastics, not algorithms</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Matrix Traversal.** In-place matrix transforms and ordered traversals: rotate, spiral, set zeroes, transpose; boundary bookkeeping is the whole problem.

**Ask yourself.**

- Can the transform decompose into simpler in-place operations (transpose + reverse)?
- What four boundaries shrink each round, and when must I stop early?
- Where can I store flags for free (first row/column) without corrupting them prematurely?

**Core idea.** Keep explicit boundaries/markers and update them in a fixed order so each cell is touched a constant number of times.

**Shape.** Rotate: transpose then reverse rows. Spiral: top/bottom/left/right, four passes, shrink, guard against double-visit. Zeroes: mark first row/col, apply, then fix first row/col.

**Complexity.** Time O(m·n); space O(1).

**Traps.**

- Double-visiting the last row/column in spiral for non-square matrices
- Overwriting marker row/column before reading it
- Rotating counter-clockwise by accident
- Layer-by-layer index errors when transpose+reverse was available

**Not this when.** Grid connectivity → graph DFS/BFS. Counting paths → 2-D DP. Searching words → backtracking.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-matrix-traversal">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-sliding-window">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'substring', 'subarray', 'contiguous', 'window', 'at most k', 'without repeating', 'containing all' · A validity condition that can be updated incrementally when one element enters or leaves · O(n) expected over strings/arrays</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Sliding Window.** 'Longest/shortest/max/min contiguous subarray or substring satisfying a condition' over a linear sequence.

**Ask yourself.**

- What makes a window valid, and can I check that in O(1) with counters?
- Fixed size or variable size window?
- When the window becomes invalid, how far must the left edge move — one step, or jump?

**Core idea.** Maintain a window and O(1)-updatable summary (counts, max, distinct count) so that each element enters once and leaves once.

**Shape.** right expands one at a time; update summary; while invalid: shrink left and update; record best when valid (longest: after shrink; shortest: while valid).

**Complexity.** Time O(n) (each index enters and leaves once); space O(alphabet) or O(k).

**Traps.**

- Shrinking by one when a jump (via last-seen index) is correct
- Recording the answer at the wrong moment (before/after fixing validity)
- For 'shortest' problems, forgetting to shrink while still valid
- Windows over negative numbers break monotonicity (then prefix sums, not windows)

**Not this when.** Elements not contiguous → DP/hashing. Condition not incrementally maintainable (e.g., median) → different structure. Negative numbers with sum constraint → prefix sums + hashing.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-sliding-window">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-stack">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'valid parentheses', 'balanced', 'nested', 'undo', 'evaluate expression', 'next greater/smaller' · The answer for an element depends on the nearest previous element with some property · Need to process in LIFO order</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Stack.** Matching/nesting, 'most recent unmatched thing', next-greater-element, or simulating recursion iteratively.

**Ask yourself.**

- What is the most recent open item that the current item must pair with?
- Should the stack hold values or indices (indices when distances/spans matter)?
- Is a monotonic stack (increasing/decreasing) what I need for 'next greater'?

**Core idea.** The stack holds exactly the unresolved candidates; the top is always the one the current element interacts with.

**Shape.** For each element: pop while top is resolved by it (recording answers); push the element; at the end handle leftovers.

**Complexity.** Time O(n) (each element pushed/popped once); space O(n).

**Traps.**

- Popping from an empty stack
- Not checking the stack is empty at the end (unmatched openers)
- Storing values when indices are needed
- Confusing which direction a monotonic stack should be monotonic

**Not this when.** FIFO order needed → queue/BFS. Need min/max over a sliding window → deque. Random access needed → arrays.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-stack">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-topological-sort">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'prerequisites', 'dependencies', 'order', 'schedule', 'alien dictionary', 'build order' · Directed edges meaning 'must come before' · Ask 'is there a cycle?' in a directed graph</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Topological Sort.** Directed dependencies: can all tasks finish, in what order, is there a cycle, derive an order from pairwise constraints.

**Ask yourself.**

- Where do the edges come from (given, or derived from adjacent comparisons)?
- Kahn's (indegree + queue) or DFS with three colours?
- What does a cycle mean for the answer (impossible / empty)?
- Are there nodes with no edges that still need to appear?

**Core idea.** A node can be emitted once all its predecessors are; if some nodes never reach indegree 0, there is a cycle.

**Shape.** Build adjacency + indegree → queue all indegree-0 → pop, emit, decrement neighbours, push zeros → emitted count == n else cycle.

**Complexity.** Time O(V+E); space O(V+E).

**Traps.**

- Edge direction reversed
- Plain visited set (cannot distinguish cycle from cross edge) — use 3 colours
- Forgetting isolated nodes
- Alien dictionary: prefix case ('abc' before 'ab') is invalid; multiple valid orders

**Not this when.** Undirected graph → components/union-find. Need shortest path → BFS/Dijkstra. Order not constrained → sorting.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-topological-sort">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-tree-bfs">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'level order', 'level by level', 'each level', 'minimum depth', 'width' · Need nodes grouped by distance from the root</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Tree BFS.** Level-order questions: levels as lists, right-side view, minimum depth, zigzag, connecting nodes on the same level.

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I delimit one level in the queue (snapshot len(queue))?
- Do I need per-level aggregation or just order?
- Would DFS with a depth parameter be equally simple?

**Core idea.** A queue processes nodes in distance order; processing exactly len(queue) nodes handles one level.

**Shape.** queue=[root]; while queue: size=len(queue); for _ in range(size): pop, record, push children; append level result.

**Complexity.** Time O(n); space O(w) where w is max width (up to n/2).

**Traps.**

- Not snapshotting the level size
- Pushing None children
- Using BFS when the problem is really per-subtree (DFS simpler)

**Not this when.** Per-subtree values → DFS. Sorted order from BST → inorder DFS.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-tree-bfs">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-tree-dfs">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'binary tree', 'subtree', 'path', 'depth/height', 'same/identical', 'invert', 'maximum path sum' · The answer at a node depends only on answers from its children (post-order) · Or constraints flow down from ancestors (pre-order with parameters)</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Tree DFS.** Anything computed per subtree: depth, sums, validity, equality, paths, invert, construct. Recursion that returns a value up.

**Ask yourself.**

- What does a subtree need to return to its parent (one number? a pair? a boolean?)
- What information flows down (bounds, path so far)?
- Is the global answer different from the returned value (path sum problems)?

**Core idea.** Post-order recursion: solve children first, combine at the node; keep a separate global when the answer is not what you pass upward.

**Shape.** def dfs(node): if not node: base; L = dfs(left); R = dfs(right); update global; return combined-for-parent.

**Complexity.** Time O(n); space O(h) recursion (worst O(n) skewed).

**Traps.**

- Returning the two-branch path upward (only one branch can continue)
- Not clamping negative contributions to 0 where allowed
- Checking only immediate children for BST validity instead of propagated bounds
- Recursion depth on skewed trees (use iterative if huge)

**Not this when.** Need level-by-level order or shortest path in an unweighted tree → BFS. Need sorted order from a BST → inorder.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-tree-dfs">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-trie">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'prefix', 'autocomplete', 'dictionary of words', 'startsWith', 'many words on a grid' · Repeated prefix checks that would re-scan strings</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Trie.** Prefix operations over many words: insert/search/startsWith, wildcard search, finding all dictionary words in a grid.

**Ask yourself.**

- What does a node store — children map and an end-of-word flag (or the word itself)?
- How does a wildcard branch (DFS over all children)?
- Can the trie prune a search (stop when no child matches)?

**Core idea.** Shared prefixes are stored once; walking one character per level makes prefix queries O(L).

**Shape.** Node = {children: {}, end: bool}; insert walks/creates; search walks; startsWith walks without end check; DFS for wildcards.

**Complexity.** Time O(L) per operation; space O(total characters).

**Traps.**

- Confusing search (needs end flag) with startsWith
- Not pruning found words / dead leaves in grid search (TLE)
- Duplicate results when a word is found via two paths
- Recursion depth for long words is fine; grid DFS unmark is the usual bug

**Not this when.** Single string matching → hashing/KMP. Suffix queries → suffix structures. Few words → a set is enough.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-trie">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-two-pointers">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'sorted array', 'palindrome', 'pair/triplet', 'container', 'in place' · A monotonic relationship: moving one pointer changes the quantity in a predictable direction · Need O(1) extra space</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Two Pointers.** Sorted (or sortable) sequences, palindromes, or 'pick two elements' questions where a brute-force pair scan is O(n²).

**Ask yourself.**

- If I fix one end, can I discard a whole side of candidates by a single comparison?
- Do the pointers converge (ends inward) or chase (same direction, fast/slow)?
- Can sorting first unlock the monotonicity?

**Core idea.** Each pointer move provably discards candidates that cannot beat the current best, so every element is visited O(1) times.

**Shape.** Sort if needed → place pointers → loop while they have not crossed → compare, record, move the pointer whose move can improve the answer.

**Complexity.** Time O(n) after an O(n log n) sort; space O(1).

**Traps.**

- Moving the wrong pointer (the one whose move cannot improve the result)
- Duplicate handling in k-sum problems
- Off-by-one on the crossing condition
- Forgetting to skip invalid characters (palindromes)

**Not this when.** Need to consider a contiguous range with a running property → sliding window. Need arbitrary lookups in unsorted data → hashing.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-two-pointers">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="cp-union-find">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN · CUES</span><span class="rev-q">'connected components', 'valid tree', 'redundant connection', 'union', 'group' · Edges arrive as a list and only connectivity matters, not paths · Undirected</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Union Find (Disjoint Set Union).** Dynamic connectivity: count components, detect a cycle in an undirected graph, check if edges form a tree, group equivalent items.

**Ask yourself.**

- Does each successful union reduce the component count by one?
- Does a failed union (same root) mean a cycle?
- Do I need path compression/union by rank (yes, it is two lines)?

**Core idea.** Each set has one representative; find returns it in near-O(1) amortised; union merges sets or reveals a cycle.

**Shape.** parent=[i]; find with path compression; union returns False if same root; components = n − successful unions.

**Complexity.** Time O((V+E) α(n)) ≈ linear; space O(V).

**Traps.**

- No path compression (still passes but say why it matters)
- Forgetting the edge-count check for trees (n−1 edges AND connected)
- Using it on directed graphs (wrong tool)

**Not this when.** Directed dependencies → topological sort. Need the actual path → DFS/BFS. Need to un-union → offline tricks (rare).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="cp-union-find">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: 1-D Dynamic Programming (10)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-climbing-stairs">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Climbing Stairs: 'distinct ways to reach the top', steps of 1 or 2</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 1-D DP (Fibonacci recurrence)

**Ask yourself.**

- What was the last step?

**The leap.** ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2); two rolling variables suffice.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Recursion without memoisation; base cases.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-climbing-stairs">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-coin-change">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Coin Change: 'fewest coins to make amount', 'infinite supply', 'return −1 if impossible'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 1-D DP, unbounded knapsack (minimum)

**Ask yourself.**

- Is greedy by largest coin correct? (no — find the counterexample)
- Which smaller amounts does dp[amount] depend on?

**The leap.** dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a − c]) over coins; fill amounts bottom-up with an infinity sentinel.

**Complexity.** O(amount × coins) time, O(amount) space.

**Trap.** Greedy; mishandling the impossible sentinel.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-coin-change">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-decode-ways">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Decode Ways: 'digits to letters', 'number of ways to decode', zeros</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 1-D DP (Fibonacci-like with validity checks)

**Ask yourself.**

- What are the last one or two digits I could have consumed?
- Which two-digit values are valid (10-26), and when is a single '0' invalid?

**The leap.** ways(i) = (valid one-digit ? ways(i − 1) : 0) + (valid two-digit ? ways(i − 2) : 0).

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Leading zeros; '30'-style invalid pairs; a lone '0'.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-decode-ways">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-house-robber-ii">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">House Robber II: 'houses arranged in a circle'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 1-D DP on a circular array (two linear passes)

**Ask yourself.**

- What single new constraint does the circle add?

**The leap.** First and last cannot both be taken: answer = max(rob(houses[1:]), rob(houses[:-1])).

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Forgetting the single-house case; trying to rotate the array.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-house-robber-ii">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-house-robber">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">House Robber: 'cannot rob adjacent houses', 'maximum amount'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 1-D DP (take / skip)

**Ask yourself.**

- At house i, what are the two choices and what earlier states do they depend on?

**The leap.** best(i) = max(best(i − 1), best(i − 2) + value[i]); roll two variables.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Greedy picking of alternates; off-by-one on the first two houses.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-house-robber">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-longest-increasing-subsequence">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Longest Increasing Subsequence: 'longest strictly increasing subsequence' (not contiguous)</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 1-D DP O(n²)

**Ask yourself.**

- dp[i] = LIS ending at i — which j feed it?
- What sorted array of 'tails' would let me binary search instead?

**The leap.** dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]; or maintain the smallest tail per length and binary search.

**Complexity.** O(n²) or O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Confusing subsequence with subarray; bisect side for strict increase.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-longest-increasing-subsequence">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-longest-palindromic-substring">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Longest Palindromic Substring: 'longest palindromic substring'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Expand around center

**Ask yourself.**

- How many centers are there (odd and even)?
- Can I expand outward from each center and keep the best?

**The leap.** Every palindrome has a center; expand from each of the 2n − 1 centers while the ends match.

**Complexity.** O(n²) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Forgetting even-length centers; returning the length instead of the substring.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-longest-palindromic-substring">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-maximum-product-subarray">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Maximum Product Subarray: 'maximum product of a contiguous subarray', negatives and zeros</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 1-D DP tracking max and min

**Ask yourself.**

- Why is Kadane's single running value not enough?
- What does a negative number do to the current minimum?

**The leap.** Track both the current maximum and minimum products, because a negative flips them; zero resets both.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Tracking only the max; forgetting to swap when the element is negative.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-maximum-product-subarray">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-palindromic-substrings">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Palindromic Substrings: 'count palindromic substrings'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Expand around center (counting)

**Ask yourself.**

- Same centers as the longest-palindrome problem — what do I count on each successful expansion?

**The leap.** Each successful expansion step from a center is one more palindrome.

**Complexity.** O(n²) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Double counting; missing even centers.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-palindromic-substrings">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-word-break">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Word Break: 'can s be segmented into dictionary words'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 1-D DP over prefixes

**Ask yourself.**

- Define dp[i] as 'prefix of length i is segmentable' — which j make it true?
- Can I bound j by the longest word length?

**The leap.** dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] true and s[j:i] in the dictionary.

**Complexity.** O(n²) time (or O(n × maxLen)), O(n) space.

**Trap.** Greedy longest-match; recomputing without memoisation.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-word-break">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: 2-D Dynamic Programming (2)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-count-paths">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Unique Paths: 'paths from top-left to bottom-right', 'only right or down'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 2-D grid DP

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I arrive at cell (i, j)?
- Is one row of state enough?

**The leap.** paths(i, j) = paths(i − 1, j) + paths(i, j − 1); a single rolling row suffices; also C(m + n − 2, m − 1).

**Complexity.** O(m·n) time, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Edge initialisation.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-count-paths">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-longest-common-subsequence">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Longest Common Subsequence: 'two strings', 'longest common subsequence' (not substring)</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** 2-D DP over two sequences

**Ask yourself.**

- What happens when the last characters match? When they do not?

**The leap.** dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i − 1][j − 1] on a match, else max(dp[i − 1][j], dp[i][j − 1]).

**Complexity.** O(m·n) time, O(m·n) space (or O(min(m, n)) rolled).

**Trap.** Subsequence vs substring; padding off-by-one.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-longest-common-subsequence">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Advanced Graphs (1)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-foreign-dictionary">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · HARD</span><span class="rev-q">Alien Dictionary: 'order of letters from a sorted list of words', 'return empty if invalid', 'hard'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Topological sort from derived constraints

**Ask yourself.**

- Where do edges come from? (first differing character of adjacent words)
- What makes the input invalid — cycles, and what else? (a word before its own prefix)

**The leap.** Adjacent words yield one edge each from their first differing characters; topologically sort all letters, including those with no edges.

**Complexity.** O(total characters + V + E) time, O(V + E) space.

**Trap.** Missing the prefix-invalid case; forgetting isolated letters; assuming a unique order.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-foreign-dictionary">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Arrays & Hashing (8)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-anagram-groups">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Group Anagrams: 'group the anagrams together' · Many strings, output as groups</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Arrays / Hashing (canonical key → bucket)

**Ask yourself.**

- What canonical form identifies an anagram class?
- Sorted string (k log k) or 26-count tuple (k) as the key?

**The leap.** Map each word to a canonical signature; the map's values are the groups.

**Complexity.** O(n·k) with count-tuple keys, O(n·k log k) with sorted keys; O(n·k) space.

**Trap.** Using a list as a dictionary key; over-thinking output order (any order is fine).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-anagram-groups">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-duplicate-integer">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Contains Duplicate: 'any value appears at least twice' · Unsorted array, existence question, expected O(n)</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Arrays / Hashing (set membership)

**Ask yourself.**

- Do I need positions, or only whether something was seen before?
- If extra space were forbidden, would sorting be acceptable?

**The leap.** A hash set answers 'have I seen this?' in O(1); one scan with an early exit.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(n) space (sort variant: O(n log n), O(1)).

**Trap.** Nested-loop comparison, or comparing set length to array length without thinking about early exit.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-duplicate-integer">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-is-anagram">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Valid Anagram: Two strings, 'rearranged', 'same letters' · Small fixed alphabet mentioned or implied</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Arrays / Hashing (frequency count)

**Ask yourself.**

- Does a length mismatch end it immediately?
- Is the alphabet fixed (array of 26) or arbitrary (map)?

**The leap.** Two strings are anagrams iff their letter multisets are equal: compare frequency counts, not orderings.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space for a fixed alphabet.

**Trap.** Sorting both strings works but is O(n log n); assuming lowercase ASCII when Unicode is allowed.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-is-anagram">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-longest-consecutive-sequence">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Longest Consecutive Sequence: 'longest consecutive elements sequence', unsorted, 'O(n)'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Arrays / Hashing (sequence-start detection)

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I avoid re-counting the middle of a run?
- What identifies the start of a run? (its predecessor is absent)

**The leap.** Put everything in a set; only count upward from numbers whose predecessor is missing, so every element is walked once.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(n) space (sort alternative O(n log n)).

**Trap.** Counting from every number gives O(n²) on long runs; forgetting duplicates when sorting.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-longest-consecutive-sequence">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-products-of-array-discluding-self">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Product of Array Except Self: 'product of all elements except nums[i]', 'without division', 'O(n)'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Prefix / suffix accumulation

**Ask yourself.**

- What does everything to the left of i contribute? Everything to the right?
- Can the output array hold the prefix pass while a scalar carries the suffix?

**The leap.** answer[i] = (product of prefix before i) × (product of suffix after i); two passes, the second folding the suffix into a running scalar.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) extra space (output excluded).

**Trap.** Division breaks on zeros; off-by-one between exclusive and inclusive prefix.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-products-of-array-discluding-self">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-string-encode-and-decode">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Encode and Decode Strings: 'encode a list of strings to one string and decode back', 'any characters may appear'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Design / string framing (length prefix)

**Ask yourself.**

- Is there any delimiter that cannot appear in the input?
- How does the decoder know where each string ends without scanning for a delimiter?

**The leap.** Length-prefix framing: write the length, a separator, then the payload — the decoder reads the length and jumps; exactly how wire protocols avoid escaping.

**Complexity.** O(total length) both directions, O(1) extra beyond output.

**Trap.** Choosing a delimiter character and then needing escaping; forgetting multi-digit lengths.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-string-encode-and-decode">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-top-k-elements-in-list">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Top K Frequent Elements: 'k most frequent', 'answer is unique', 'better than O(n log n)'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Arrays / Hashing + bucket sort

**Ask yourself.**

- Do I need a full sort, or only the top k?
- Frequencies are bounded by n — can a frequency be an array index?
- Heap of size k: what polarity, what tuple?

**The leap.** Count, then place values into buckets indexed by frequency and read from the top; or keep a size-k heap.

**Complexity.** O(n) bucket approach, O(n log k) heap; O(n) space.

**Trap.** Sorting all pairs by count when the problem asks for better; building a max-heap when a min-heap of size k is intended (or vice versa).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-top-k-elements-in-list">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-two-integer-sum">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Two Sum: 'two numbers that add up to target', 'return indices' · Unsorted, exactly one answer</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Arrays / Hashing (complement lookup)

**Ask yourself.**

- Is the array sorted? (then converging pointers)
- For element x, what do I wish I knew instantly? (whether target − x was seen)
- Can an element pair with itself?

**The leap.** While scanning, look up the complement in a value→index map; insert the current element only after the lookup.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Inserting before checking (pairs an element with itself); sorting destroys the required indices.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-two-integer-sum">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Backtracking (2)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-combination-target-sum">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Combination Sum: 'all unique combinations that sum to target', 'may be used unlimited times'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Backtracking with unlimited reuse

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I prevent the same combination appearing in a different order?
- When can I prune a branch?

**The leap.** Iterate candidates from a start index (never backwards) to enforce non-decreasing order; recurse with the same index to allow reuse; prune when the remainder goes negative.

**Complexity.** Exponential time (roughly O(k^(T/min))), O(T/min) depth.

**Trap.** Producing permutations instead of combinations; no pruning.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-combination-target-sum">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-search-for-word">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Word Search: 'word exists in the grid', 'adjacent cells', 'cannot reuse a cell'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Backtracking on a grid (DFS)

**Ask yourself.**

- What is the state of one DFS step (cell, index into word)?
- How do I mark visited cheaply and undo it?

**The leap.** From each cell matching the first letter, DFS over 4 neighbours matching the next letter; mark in place and unmark on return.

**Complexity.** O(m·n·4^L) time worst case, O(L) space.

**Trap.** Forgetting to unmark; allowing diagonal moves; not stopping at the first success.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-search-for-word">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Binary Search (2)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Find Minimum In Rotated Sorted Array: 'rotated', 'sorted', 'O(log n)', 'minimum'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Binary Search on a rotated array

**Ask yourself.**

- Which half is sorted at mid, and where can the minimum live?
- Compare mid with the right end or the left end?

**The leap.** If nums[mid] > nums[right] the minimum is right of mid; otherwise it is mid or to the left — halve accordingly.

**Complexity.** O(log n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Comparing with the left end (fails when not rotated); off-by-one when shrinking toward mid.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-find-target-in-rotated-sorted-array">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Search In Rotated Sorted Array: 'rotated sorted array', 'find target', 'O(log n)'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Binary Search with sorted-half detection

**Ask yourself.**

- At mid, which half is definitely sorted?
- Is the target inside that sorted half's range? If not, go to the other.

**The leap.** One half around mid is always sorted; test membership in the sorted half to decide the direction.

**Complexity.** O(log n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Boundary conditions with ≤ vs <; finding the pivot first is a valid two-step alternative but longer.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-find-target-in-rotated-sorted-array">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Bit Manipulation (5)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-counting-bits">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Counting Bits: 'number of 1 bits for every i from 0 to n', 'O(n)'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** DP over bits

**Ask yourself.**

- How does i relate to i >> 1 or to i & (i − 1)?

**The leap.** count[i] = count[i & (i − 1)] + 1 (or count[i >> 1] + (i & 1)).

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Running popcount per number (fine, but misses the DP point).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-counting-bits">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-missing-number">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Missing Number: 'n distinct numbers in range 0..n', 'find the missing one'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** XOR / arithmetic sum

**Ask yourself.**

- What cancels out if I combine indices and values?

**The leap.** XOR all indices 0..n with all values leaves the missing number; or n(n + 1)/2 minus the sum.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Sorting (unnecessary O(n log n)).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-missing-number">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-number-of-one-bits">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Number of 1 Bits: 'number of 1 bits', 'Hamming weight'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Bit manipulation (clear lowest set bit)

**Ask yourself.**

- What does n & (n − 1) do to n?

**The leap.** n & (n − 1) clears the lowest set bit; count the iterations until zero.

**Complexity.** O(number of set bits) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Negative numbers / unbounded integers in Python.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-number-of-one-bits">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-reverse-bits">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Reverse Bits: 'reverse the 32 bits'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Bit manipulation loop

**Ask yourself.**

- How does bit i move to position 31 − i?

**The leap.** Shift the result left and OR in the input's lowest bit, 32 times.

**Complexity.** O(32) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Python's unbounded integers (mask to 32 bits).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-reverse-bits">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-sum-of-two-integers">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Sum of Two Integers: 'add two integers without + or −'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Bitwise addition (XOR + carry)

**Ask yourself.**

- What do XOR and AND-shifted-left represent in addition?

**The leap.** sum = a ^ b, carry = (a & b) << 1; repeat until the carry is zero, masking to 32 bits in Python.

**Complexity.** O(32) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Infinite loops with Python negatives when not masked.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-sum-of-two-integers">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Graphs (6)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-clone-graph">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Clone Graph: 'deep copy of a connected graph', neighbours lists, cycles</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Graph DFS / BFS with an old→new map

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I avoid infinite recursion on cycles?
- Where do I keep the mapping from original to clone?

**The leap.** A hash map from original node to its clone doubles as the visited set; create the clone before recursing into neighbours.

**Complexity.** O(V + E) time, O(V) space.

**Trap.** Creating duplicate clones; not handling an empty graph.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-clone-graph">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-count-connected-components">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Number of Connected Components In An Undirected Graph: 'number of connected components', undirected edges</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Union Find

**Ask yourself.**

- Starting from n components, what does each successful union do?

**The leap.** Components = n minus the number of unions that actually merged two different sets.

**Complexity.** O(E α(n)) time, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Building adjacency for DFS when union-find is shorter; skipping path compression is fine but say why it matters.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-count-connected-components">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-count-number-of-islands">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Number of Islands: 'count islands', grid of 1s and 0s, 4-directional</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Grid DFS / BFS flood fill

**Ask yourself.**

- What is a node and what is an edge here?
- How do I mark visited (in place or a set)?

**The leap.** Each unvisited land cell starts a flood fill that sinks the whole island; count the fills.

**Complexity.** O(m·n) time, O(m·n) worst-case space.

**Trap.** Recursion depth on large grids; diagonal adjacency.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-count-number-of-islands">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-course-schedule">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Course Schedule: 'prerequisites', 'can you finish all courses'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Topological sort / cycle detection in a directed graph

**Ask yourself.**

- Is this simply 'does the directed graph contain a cycle'?
- Three-colour DFS or Kahn's indegree queue?

**The leap.** A valid order exists iff there is no directed cycle: detect via DFS states (visiting/visited) or by checking that Kahn's algorithm processes every node.

**Complexity.** O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space.

**Trap.** A plain visited set cannot distinguish a back edge from a cross edge; reversed edge direction.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-course-schedule">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-pacific-atlantic-water-flow">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Pacific Atlantic Water Flow: 'water can flow to both oceans', heights, 'flows to equal or lower'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Multi-source reverse DFS / BFS from the borders

**Ask yourself.**

- Simulate from every cell, or reverse the flow from each ocean's border?
- Which comparison direction do I use when climbing?

**The leap.** Start from each ocean's border cells and climb to cells with height ≥ current; the answer is the intersection of the two reachable sets.

**Complexity.** O(m·n) time, O(m·n) space.

**Trap.** Forward simulation per cell (quadratic); reversing the height comparison incorrectly.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-pacific-atlantic-water-flow">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-valid-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Graph Valid Tree: 'n nodes and a list of edges', 'valid tree'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Union Find (or DFS) + edge count

**Ask yourself.**

- What two properties define a tree on n nodes?

**The leap.** Exactly n − 1 edges and fully connected (equivalently: connected and acyclic).

**Complexity.** O(n α(n)) time, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Checking only connectivity or only the edge count; undirected DFS needs parent tracking to avoid false cycles.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-valid-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Greedy (2)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-jump-game">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Jump Game: 'can you reach the last index', 'maximum jump length'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Greedy farthest-reach

**Ask yourself.**

- What is the farthest index reachable so far?
- When exactly am I stuck?

**The leap.** Track the farthest reachable index; if the current index exceeds it, fail; or move the goal leftward from the end.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Quadratic DP; confusing with the minimum-jumps variant.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-jump-game">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-maximum-subarray">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Maximum Subarray: 'maximum sum of a contiguous subarray'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Kadane's algorithm (greedy / DP)

**Ask yourself.**

- At each element: extend the current run or start fresh?
- When does a prefix stop being useful?

**The leap.** current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]); a negative running sum never helps.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Initialising to 0 when all numbers may be negative.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-maximum-subarray">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Heap / Priority Queue (1)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-find-median-in-a-data-stream">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · HARD</span><span class="rev-q">Find Median From Data Stream: 'stream', 'median at any time', 'addNum / findMedian'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Two heaps (max-heap low half, min-heap high half)

**Ask yourself.**

- Which structure keeps the middle available after O(log n) insertions?
- How do I keep the two halves balanced?

**The leap.** Split the numbers into a lower half (max-heap) and upper half (min-heap) whose sizes differ by at most one; the median is at the tops.

**Complexity.** O(log n) per insert, O(1) per median, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Min-heap-only library (negate for the max-heap); rebalancing in the wrong direction.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-find-median-in-a-data-stream">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Intervals (5)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-insert-new-interval">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Insert Interval: 'sorted non-overlapping intervals', 'insert and merge if necessary'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Interval linear scan (three phases)

**Ask yourself.**

- Which intervals end before the new one, which overlap, which start after?

**The leap.** Append everything ending before; merge everything overlapping into the new interval; append the rest.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Wrong overlap condition; forgetting to append the new interval when it belongs at the end.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-insert-new-interval">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-meeting-schedule-ii">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Meeting Rooms II: 'minimum number of conference rooms'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sweep line (sorted starts and ends)

**Ask yourself.**

- How many meetings are in progress at any instant?
- Sort starts and ends separately, or keep a heap of end times?

**The leap.** Rooms = maximum concurrency: +1 at each start, −1 at each end (or the heap size after popping finished meetings).

**Complexity.** O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Tie order when a meeting ends exactly as another starts; reusing the Meeting Rooms logic.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-meeting-schedule-ii">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-meeting-schedule">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Meeting Rooms: 'can a person attend all meetings'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sort + adjacent overlap check

**Ask yourself.**

- After sorting by start, what must hold for every adjacent pair?

**The leap.** Any start earlier than the previous end is a conflict.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Boundary semantics when one meeting ends exactly as another starts.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-meeting-schedule">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-merge-intervals">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Merge Intervals: 'merge all overlapping intervals'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sort by start + sweep

**Ask yourself.**

- After sorting by start, when does the current interval overlap the last merged one?

**The leap.** If start ≤ last.end, extend last.end to the max; otherwise start a new interval.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

**Trap.** Not taking the max of ends; inclusive vs exclusive touching.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-merge-intervals">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-non-overlapping-intervals">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Non Overlapping Intervals: 'minimum number of intervals to remove'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Greedy by earliest end

**Ask yourself.**

- When two intervals overlap, which one should I keep?

**The leap.** Keep the interval that ends earliest (it leaves the most room); count the others as removals.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Sorting by start and keeping the longer; not seeing the equivalence with maximum non-overlapping set.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-non-overlapping-intervals">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Linked List (6)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-linked-list-cycle-detection">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Linked List Cycle: 'cycle', 'constant memory'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Fast / slow pointers (Floyd)

**Ask yourself.**

- Why must a fast pointer meet a slow one inside a cycle?
- What null checks does the fast pointer need?

**The leap.** A pointer moving two steps gains one node per iteration on a pointer moving one; inside a cycle they must meet.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Missing fast.next null checks; using a set when O(1) space was expected.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-linked-list-cycle-detection">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-merge-k-sorted-linked-lists">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · HARD</span><span class="rev-q">Merge K Sorted Lists: 'k sorted lists', 'merge all'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Heap (k-way merge)

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I pick the global minimum among k heads cheaply?
- Does pairwise merging in log k rounds give the same complexity?

**The leap.** A min-heap over the k current heads yields the next element in O(log k); or merge lists in pairs, halving the count each round.

**Complexity.** O(N log k) time, O(k) space (pairwise: O(N log k), O(1)).

**Trap.** Sequential merging is O(N·k); heap tuples need an index tie-breaker because nodes are not comparable.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-merge-k-sorted-linked-lists">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-merge-two-sorted-linked-lists">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Merge Two Sorted Lists: 'two sorted linked lists', 'merge into one sorted list'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Two-pointer merge with dummy head

**Ask yourself.**

- Does a dummy head remove the head special case?
- What happens to the remainder of the longer list?

**The leap.** Splice existing nodes by comparison behind a dummy head; attach the leftover tail.

**Complexity.** O(n + m) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Allocating new nodes; forgetting the leftover tail.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-merge-two-sorted-linked-lists">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-remove-node-from-end-of-linked-list">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Remove Nth Node From End of List: 'nth node from the end', 'one pass'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Two pointers with a fixed gap

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I place one pointer n steps ahead of another?
- What if the node to remove is the head?

**The leap.** Start a lead pointer n+1 ahead from a dummy; when it reaches the end, the trailing pointer is just before the target.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Trap.** Removing the head without a dummy; off-by-one in the gap.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-remove-node-from-end-of-linked-list">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>
